questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Patronage and the subject of a picture
questions.learningObjective: state how a patron's needs constrain a commission
questions.stem: A committee pays for a large picture to hang in a public hall, while the painter would rather paint something smaller and less predictable. Whose decision settles the subject and the size of the work?

options.text: The patron's, since the commission fixes the purpose, the room and the sum available
The painter's, since only the artist can judge what belongs in a hall of that kind
options.misconception: believes the painter decides the subject regardless of who is paying

options.text: The committee's by voting, since a committee always overrides a single painter
options.misconception: reduces the question to a vote and ignores what the payment buys

options.text: Nobody's, since the size and subject of a picture are settled by convention alone
options.misconception: attributes the decision to custom and leaves the paying party out of it

questions.explanation: Patronage is the controlling relationship in most pre-modern art, because the person paying decides what the picture is for, and the purpose fixes the subject, the scale, the material, the price and the place where the work will be seen. A hall, a chapel, a private devotions and a market are four different problems, and the same painter answers them in four different ways. Records of contracts, letters and payments survive often enough to show that the terms were negotiated rather than simply obeyed, but the terms set the limits inside which the negotiation took place.
questions.hint: Ask who pays, and what the money is being bought.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission and its stated purpose
questions.learningObjective: apply a commission's stated purpose to the format of a work
questions.stem: A contract for an altarpiece states that the work is to stand at the high altar of a chapel, is to be seen from the nave, and is paid for by the guild that endowed the chapel. What follows from those terms?

options.text: The picture has to be large enough to be read at a distance, bought by a body with a stake in display
The painter may settle the size later, since the guild that paid the bill took charge of it afterwards
options.misconception: believes the payer leaves the scale open after agreeing a fixed location

options.text: The work has to be portable, since a guild's property was carried in procession each year
options.misconception: misreads a fixed altar commission as though it were a processional banner

options.text: The subject is the painter's own choice, because the contract says nothing about the subject at all
options.misconception: treats silence in a contract as permission to ignore every other constraint

questions.explanation: The stated purpose is doing the work here. A picture at a high altar is seen from a distance, in bad light, and often with people standing between the viewer and it, so its scale and the clarity of its main figures follow from that. The payment matters as much as the location, because a guild that has endowed a chapel has an interest in being seen as the founder of it. Contracts of this kind exist in quantity and are the plainest documentary evidence we have of patronage as a working relationship rather than as a later assumption.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer in a nave can see of a picture at the far end of a chapel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify what makes a church image legible
questions.stem: Most of the people who entered a large medieval church could not read, so the images there had to teach without words. Which set of devices does that work?

options.text: Fixed attributes and gestures, with rank shown by size and by height in the picture, so figures read at a glance
Inscriptions naming each figure in Latin, so the congregation could learn who was who
options.misconception: relies on writing for an audience that the picture exists precisely to serve without it

options.text: Realistic relative size, so that a nearer figure is painted larger exactly as the eye would see it
options.misconception: mistakes optical accuracy for a device of legibility and reverses its purpose

options.text: A single scene carrying the whole story at once, so nobody has to read it in sequence
options.misconception: supposes legibility comes from completeness rather than from convention

questions.explanation: The conventions of church imagery are a system for identification in a largely non-reading audience. Attributes are fixed and unmistakable: a key, a sword, a wound, an animal, a wheel. Gestures and postures are equally conventional, as is the frontal presentation that gives a saint his stillness and authority. Rank is carried by size and by the tier a figure occupies, so the arrangement itself states the order of the church. What the system does not do is describe a place or a moment; the same set of figures and attributes can be rearranged to tell very different stories, which is what makes the imagery flexible enough to cover a whole cycle.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer needs in order to name a figure without being able to read a label.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the function of a donor image and its inscription
questions.stem: A carved panel shows a large holy figure, and at the bottom corner a much smaller man kneeling in plain clothes, with a painted strip naming him and naming the saint above him. What are the strip and the small figure doing?

options.text: They record the payment and present the donor as someone introduced to the saint, not as an equal
They are a later addition, since a patron was never shown inside a church picture at all
options.misconception: denies a standard practice in which donors appear at the scale of their importance

options.text: They name the carpenter and the master of the workshop, so the trade is kept informed
options.misconception: reads a devotional inscription as a record of the makers

options.text: They prove the work was made for a private house, since churches never allowed donors in
options.misconception: concludes a domestic destination from the presence of a donor

questions.explanation: The scale difference states rank, and the kneeling gesture states what the donor wants from the saint, which is that the prayer be heard. A saint is often made to introduce the donor, standing between him and the one he addresses, which is a compact way of saying that the gift has been placed in the right hands. The painted inscription then supplies the information the scale cannot: the name of the man, and the name of the saint to whom the work is dedicated. Together they fix the work as a particular gift, in a particular chapel, made in a particular year.
questions.hint: Ask what the difference in size between the two figures is asserting, and what the strip adds to it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A court image and its political claim
questions.learningObjective: infer the claim made by a court commission
questions.stem: A court painter is instructed to place the ruler's family among figures dressed as gods, and to make the ruler the largest figure on the wall. What political claim is the finished image making?

options.text: That the family's rule is sanctioned from above and belongs to a timeless and divinely ordered world
That the family seized its power by force, and the image records the violence of the seizure
options.misconception: reads a claim of legitimacy as a confession of a coup

options.text: That the ruler is a god in the strict sense, so the court can be worshipped outside the capital
options.misconception: takes the borrowed costume as a literal claim of divinity

options.text: That the family means to surrender its rule shortly, and the gods are being asked to approve it
options.misconception: inverts the direction of the claim, which asserts permanence rather than giving it up

questions.explanation: The image borrows the attributes of a timeless order and applies them to a living family, and the effect is to present a particular claim as though it were natural law. Scale and centrality supply the precedence that the costume cannot: the ruler is largest and nearest the centre, so the eye takes the importance as a fact about the arrangement rather than as a fact about the painting. Such pictures are instruments in an argument, and they are read by an audience that knows the politics. The work to avoid is treating them as decoration, or as evidence that anyone believed the costume literally.
questions.hint: Ask what the costume of gods and the placement of the largest figure are doing to a claim about power.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a shared period style documents
questions.stem: A group of works made within fifty years in one city share a stiff frontality, a narrow range of colours and a single preferred viewpoint. What does that shared look record about them?

options.text: The common constraints of the time and place: materials, training, patrons and the market
One painter's taste, imposed on everyone else working in that city and period
options.misconception: explains a shared style by a single personality rather than by shared conditions

options.text: A ruling taste, enforced by inspectors who rejected work that broke the rules
options.misconception: assumes an enforcement body that was not part of artistic production

options.text: The copying of one older work, repeated so exactly that nothing new could develop
options.misconception: mistakes the influence of a single model for the whole of a style

questions.explanation: A period style is best understood as a set of shared constraints plus a set of shared choices. The constraints are cheap to list: the materials that could be bought, the training a workshop gave, the patrons and what they paid for, the subjects they would accept, the buildings available, the market for pictures. Within them, individual painters make decisions that differ, and those differences are as informative as the agreement, because they show what was available to vary and what was not. To call a style the product of one personality is to explain it by the thing the evidence does not describe.
questions.hint: Ask what all the makers of these works had in common besides their period.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state a documented reason for reviving an earlier style
questions.stem: In the nineteenth century artists and patrons deliberately returned to medieval forms, building new churches in them while machine production dominated ordinary goods. What explains that revival?

options.text: The medieval craft ideal was read as an argument against industrial production, and suited church work
Medieval buildings were still standing everywhere, so the old style was simply copied from them
options.misconception: assumes an abundance of intact medieval buildings that did not exist

options.text: The older painters used a better method, so the revival was an attempt to recover that method
options.misconception: believes a revival follows from technical superiority, which it did not

options.text: Patrons had run out of money, so they commissioned whatever was cheapest to build
options.misconception: reduces a cultural argument to a matter of the clients' budgets

questions.explanation: The nineteenth-century return to medieval forms is best explained by a reaction against industrial production and by the church, which had the money and the reason. Machine-made goods made the older idea of a skilled craft guild carry a new political charge, and a medieval style offered a vocabulary for objects that advertised hand work. The point to hold on to is that the revival was a modern construction: what was built in the new style was not a continuation of the old one but an argument with the present made in an old vocabulary, which is why the results differ from the buildings they admire.
questions.hint: Ask what machine production did to the value of hand-made work, and who was paying for the new churches.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The workshop and division of labour
questions.learningObjective: explain what a signature does and does not establish
questions.stem: A large painter's shop has a master who designs and supervises, assistants who prepare grounds and stretch canvases, and journeymen who execute much of the painting. What does a signature on the finished picture establish?

options.text: That the master stood behind the work and owned the design, not that his own hand painted it
That the master executed every passage, since a signature certifies the brush as well as the name
options.misconception: believes a signature is a claim about the hand rather than about responsibility

options.text: Nothing at all, since only a written contract can say who was responsible for a picture
options.misconception: denies that a signature is evidence of anything without a contract

options.text: That nobody else ever came near the picture after the master had signed and sealed it
options.misconception: reads a signature as a claim about who handled the object afterwards

questions.explanation: Workshops produce pictures collaboratively, and the division of labour is documented in contracts, inventories and account books that name assistants alongside masters. The master's contribution is normally the design, the choice of subject, the instruction and the responsibility for the result, all of which are what a signature asserts. Many of the most famous names in painting are attached to works whose surfaces are demonstrably the work of several hands, and arguments about the hand of the master are one of the standing problems of attribution. The signature is evidence of a name attached to an object, which is a different claim from evidence of a particular hand.
questions.hint: Ask what the master contributes to a shop's output, and what the signer's hand might not have done.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: identify the marks of speculatively produced work
questions.stem: A painter produces the same subject in several sizes, works quickly on some of them, and has the price set by what comparable pictures of that size fetch in the shop. What kind of production is this?

options.text: A shop making for the open market, where standard sizes and speed decide what can be sold
A single commissioned altarpiece, whose subject, size and price were all fixed by contract
options.misconception: takes a repeated subject at several sizes to be a one-off commission

options.text: A court commission, since only a court could afford a subject repeated in more than one version
options.misconception: assumes repetition is a privilege of wealthy patrons, ignoring the market trade

options.text: A private exercise, since a painter working for speed was never trying to sell the result
options.misconception: reads commercial production as work made only for the painter's own use

questions.explanation: Production for the market begins with a format the dealer already stocks and a price the buyer already expects, so the painter's first decision is how much labour the money will support. That produces the familiar marks: repeat subjects at several sizes, variable speed, uneven quality between a picture made to a deadline and one made in a slack week. It also explains why market work is sometimes the most inventive, since a painter free of a patron's subject can take the risk that a commission will not allow. A record of a sale is the clearest possible evidence that a work was made for the market.
questions.hint: Ask who decided the size and the price, and who bought the finished object.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why pictures came in standard sizes
questions.stem: Dealers preferred to handle pictures in a small number of standard sizes, and painters worked to them. What practical advantage does that give to both sides of the trade?

options.text: A dealer can stock, display and quote a known price for the format, and a painter can plan the labour
It removes any need to look at the subject, since the size alone settles what a picture is worth
options.misconception: believes a standard format makes the subject irrelevant to the price

options.text: It makes every support and frame identical, so a single maker's mould serves all of them
options.misconception: believes standardisation existed only to let makers reuse one piece of equipment

options.text: It forces every painter in a city to copy one composition in order to stay in business
options.misconception: turns a commercial convenience into a rule about what painters were allowed to invent

questions.explanation: A standard format is a piece of shared infrastructure. Canvases, stretchers and frames of a few standard sizes could be bought ready, stored, stacked and displayed, and a client could be quoted a price without a valuation. A painter who worked to those sizes could plan how many days a picture would take and which assistants to put on it, which is a large part of how a shop could meet a deadline. Standard sizes also make an inventory legible, since a list of measurements becomes a list of prices, and they are one reason the trade could function at the scale it did.
questions.hint: Ask what a dealer has to do with a picture between the time it is bought and the time it is sold.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the evidence that establishes a chain of ownership
questions.stem: An old picture has no label and no recorded history. Which combination of evidence will actually establish where it has been?

options.text: Analysis of the object itself, matched against ownership documents, inventories and sale records
The style of the picture, which fixes a period and therefore identifies the owner who bought it then
options.misconception: believes a date determines an owner, which no style can do

options.text: A family story told by the present holder, which counts once it has been written down
options.misconception: accepts an undocumented family account as equivalent to an archive

options.text: The size of the picture, since only very wealthy owners ever possessed works of that size
options.misconception: believes dimensions identify an owner rather than describing a format

questions.explanation: Provenance is established by two kinds of evidence that have to be brought together. Documents, meaning inventories, sale catalogues, correspondence, customs and export papers, tell you about ownership; physical evidence from the object, meaning its support, its ground, its pigments, its labels, its nail holes and its frame, tells you whether this object is the one those documents describe. Style alone can never do the second job, since a style dates a manner rather than an object. A chain with a gap is still evidence, and its weakness is stated rather than hidden; a chain with no documents at all is a hypothesis, however plausible.
questions.hint: Ask which evidence speaks about the object itself, and which speaks about who held it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Provenance and the history of a collection
questions.learningObjective: distinguish object provenance from collection history
questions.stem: Two things are often run together in writing about collections: the chain of owners of a single picture, and the account of how a group of pictures was gathered. How should they be separated?

options.text: Provenance is one object's chain of custody; collection history is the account of a group's making
Provenance is the history of a group, and collection history is the ownership of a single object
options.misconception: reverses the two terms, which makes every later statement about them wrong

options.text: The two are the same thing, since any collection is simply a list of its objects' owners
options.misconception: reduces a group's history to a sum of its objects' histories

options.text: Provenance concerns how the object was made, and collection history concerns what it is made of
options.misconception: assigns manufacturing and materials to the wrong one of the two

questions.explanation: Provenance is object-specific: it follows one picture through the hands of its owners, and it has legal force, because export law, restitution claims and questions of title all turn on it. The history of a collection is about the behaviour of a person or an institution over time, what they chose, what they bought, what they hung, and what they were trying to do. A picture can have a fully documented provenance and sit in a collection whose early history is unknown, and the reverse is equally possible. Keeping the two apart stops one being used to fill the gaps in the other.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two is about a single object, and which is about an institution or a person.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that no longer survives
questions.learningObjective: state what is knowable about a lost work
questions.stem: A painting appears in a seventeenth-century inventory with its subject and dimensions recorded, and a print made after it survives. What can a scholar actually establish about the picture that is lost?

options.text: That it existed, what it showed, and roughly how large it was, but nothing about how it was painted
Everything about it, because an inventory entry together with a print reproduces the object itself
options.misconception: believes a document and a copy between them restore the physical object

options.text: Nothing whatever, since a work that no longer exists cannot be reached by any method at all
options.misconception: denies that records and copies are evidence about a lost work

options.text: Only what it cost, since a recorded sale value is the single fact a lost work leaves behind
options.misconception: reduces a lost work's evidence to a price in an account book

questions.explanation: The two surviving sources answer different questions. An inventory made while the picture still existed establishes that it existed, and records its subject, its size and often the room it hung in, which is why measurements are so useful. A print, a drawing after it, or a copy establishes what it looked like from one point of view, and a print may be reversed, cropped, altered, or show the picture at an earlier date than the inventory describes. Neither source can tell you what the paint was, how thick the ground, who laid it in, or whether the hand is the one the tradition credits. The work is genuinely known and genuinely absent at the same time.
questions.hint: Ask which questions a document can answer, and which ones need the physical object in front of you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a display does to a reading
questions.learningObjective: explain how hanging works together frames a reading
questions.stem: A gallery hangs a small devotional panel beside a large narrative painting of the same event, and prints a wall text presenting the two as two treatments of one theme. What has the display done?

options.text: It has made a comparison the visitor would not otherwise make, and the text has fixed one reading of it
It has altered the two pictures, since hanging them together changes the paint in both
options.misconception: believes juxtaposition acts on the physical object rather than on the visitor

options.text: It has removed the need for a wall text, since putting works side by side explains everything
options.misconception: supposes comparison is self-explaining and needs no interpretation stated

options.text: It has restored the pictures to their original setting, since a gallery room is the maker's own room
options.misconception: claims a modern display reproduces the context the work was made for

questions.explanation: Display is interpretation, and it is a powerful one. A gallery chooses what stands beside what, the order in which rooms are walked, the height of the hang, the lighting, the spacing, the frame, and the words on the wall, and a visitor meets that sequence rather than a set of objects. The juxtaposition here asserts a shared subject, which is an argument, and the wall text then makes the argument explicit in the only form the visitor can check. The claim to avoid is that a museum is a neutral container; and the related claim, that a display restores the original context, is almost never true, because the room the work was made for is gone.
questions.hint: Ask whether a visitor would have put these two works next to each other by themselves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read a frame as evidence about an object's later history
questions.stem: A panel painting now hangs in a heavy gilded frame of the nineteenth century, cut down at the moulding so that it would fit a wall. What does that frame tell you about the object?

options.text: That it belongs to the object's later history, and that it was altered to fit a setting it was not made for
That the picture was made in the nineteenth century, since a frame dates the panel inside it
options.misconception: assumes the frame is contemporary with the object it surrounds

options.text: That the picture was always the size it is now, since a frame can only be fitted to a finished object
options.misconception: believes the frame records the original dimensions of the picture

options.text: That it says nothing at all, since a frame is separate furniture and carries no information
options.misconception: dismisses the frame as decoration and misses what it records

questions.explanation: A frame is part of the object as it has been handled, and it is evidence on at least three counts: the period and quality of the moulding, the proportions of the support, and the history of the hanging. Frames get recut, regilded and replaced as rooms change, and a cut moulding records an object being fitted to a site at the cost of losing part of the image, usually at the edges. The original frame is often lost, which is a gap in the evidence about how a work was seen. A frame is never decoration only, and it never dates the panel it holds.
questions.hint: Ask what a frame is made of, and what a cut moulding shows about the picture it surrounds.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a work enters a national collection
questions.learningObjective: identify the most transparent route of acquisition
questions.stem: A work has reached a national collection, and the question is which route leaves a record that can be checked afterwards. Which of these does?

options.text: An open purchase at a sale or from a dealer, with the price, the date and the buyer entered in a register
A removal from a private house after an owner died, with the transfer settled inside the family
options.misconception: treats an undocumented family settlement as though it were as clear as a purchase

options.text: A crate that arrived from a private collector with no papers, so the object came without a history
options.misconception: supposes an object can be acquired with no record of the transaction at all

options.text: A find in the museum's own store, where nobody ever bought it and nobody decided anything
options.misconception: credits an undocumented store transfer as though it were a recorded decision

questions.explanation: A purchase is the most transparent route because it produces a dated record with a named buyer and a sum, and a sale catalogue usually describes the object, which allows a later scholar to check whether the thing bought is the thing now held. Bequests and gifts are perfectly ordinary and often well documented, through wills and correspondence, but they depend on the survival of private papers. Acquisitions that arrive with no record of a transaction are the ones that generate later disputes, because there is nothing to test an export claim or a restitution claim against, and a public collection is judged on exactly that.
questions.hint: Ask which route produces a receipt, a date and a named buyer that can be checked later.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an artist's account of their work from later reputation
questions.stem: An artist's letters present the work as a principled reform, while a museum handbook written a century later explains the same pictures through a different theory. What is the difference between the two accounts?

options.text: The first is the artist arguing a case at the time; the second is a later reading built on a settled reputation
The first is false and the second is true, because only later writers saw the whole picture
options.misconception: treats a later account as correct because of its distance from the events

options.text: They are describing the same intentions, so any difference between them is a matter of wording
options.misconception: assumes both accounts report a single fixed intention behind the work

options.text: The first is about the pictures and the second is about the period, so the two can never overlap
options.misconception: separates the two kinds of account so far that they cannot inform each other

questions.explanation: An artist's letters, prefaces and public statements are interested documents: they are addressed to rivals, patrons and collectors at a moment when the artist's standing is still being negotiated, and they are part of the work of making a reputation. A handbook is equally constructed, but by people writing after the outcome is settled and with a canon to serve. The distance between the two is not noise to be corrected but evidence, because it shows how the work was argued for at the time and how it was later reclassified. Comparing the two is often more productive than asking which of them is right.
questions.hint: Ask who was arguing, and to whom, in each of the two texts.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state how the name of a movement comes about
questions.stem: The painters who showed together in Paris in 1874 were given a collective name that came from a journalist's mocking phrase in a review. What does that origin tell us about movement names?

options.text: Most such names are imposed afterwards by critics, and the painters themselves rarely used the word
The painters chose the name, and the journalist only repeated their own description of the group
options.misconception: credits the artists with a label that a hostile review supplied

options.text: The name was fixed by a guild rule, so the label must be official and free of critical tone
options.misconception: assumes an official body issued the term because it was mocking

options.text: The name was invented after the group had dissolved, so it cannot describe what they were doing
options.misconception: dates the naming after the event on the strength of a review published during it

questions.explanation: A movement name usually arrives from outside the group, and often from a hostile quarter: a critic's phrase, a joke, a disparaging comparison, and later adopted by the artists themselves once the phrase had proved useful in the market. The painters in this case did not set out to found a movement, and they did not use the word for themselves at the time, so the name is a later reading of what they had in common. That is not a reason to discard it, since it remains a useful shorthand, but it is a reason to ask what the name selects and what it leaves out, and to notice that adoption by the artists came after the naming.
questions.hint: Ask where the word came from first, and whether the painters were using it at the time.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why period names are retrospective
questions.stem: Words such as Renaissance and Gothic were applied to the past a long time after it happened, in several cases originally as insults. What follows from that fact about using those names?

options.text: They are useful shorthand for shared features, but they were not the past's own terms for itself
They are worthless, and no stretch of the past can be described by any label at all
options.misconception: discards a whole analytical vocabulary on the grounds that it came late

options.text: They record exactly how people at the time thought about their own work and their own age
options.misconception: reads a later retrospective word as though it were a contemporary usage

options.text: They are the most reliable evidence available, since later writers saw the whole picture at last
options.misconception: believes later writers are more reliable than the participants

questions.explanation: The words we use were coined by later writers for their own purposes, sometimes to dignify a period and sometimes to insult it, and that history is itself part of the evidence: the label tells us how the later period judged the earlier one. The names remain useful because they group works that share features which can be described, and grouping is what analysis requires. What they cannot do is report the self-understanding of the people inside the period, or draw a clean boundary, since the features they name rarely begin and end at the same moment as the label suggests.
questions.hint: Ask whether the people who made the work had a word for the period they were living in.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a manifesto gives a reader of a group's work
questions.stem: A painter publishes a text setting out what a work of art ought to be and what the artist must refuse to do. What does that text give a reader of that painter's pictures?

options.text: A stated programme to read the pictures against, including the refusals the artist claims for them
A rule book, so any painting that breaks the rule cannot be counted as a work of art
options.misconception: turns a polemic into a binding rule and makes it a test of membership

options.text: A record of the prices charged, so the pictures can be dated and placed in the market
options.misconception: supposes a statement of principles carries price and date information

options.text: A legal contract, so the claims in it can be enforced against anyone painting differently
options.misconception: reads a declaration of intent as though it created an obligation on other painters

questions.explanation: A manifesto is a public declaration of intention, addressed as much to rivals as to supporters, and it is valuable because it gives a group a criterion to be measured against. A painter who claims to refuse a particular kind of subject or effect has told us what to look for in the work, including the places where the claim is kept and the places where it is not, and the discrepancy between the two is often the most interesting thing about it. What it does not do is bind anybody else, fix a price, or date the pictures, and treating it as a rule set loses the argument it was making.
questions.hint: Ask what a manifesto asserts, and what a reader can do with the assertion.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what evidence supports an attribution
questions.stem: A work of uncertain authorship has no documents behind it. A scholar compares the handling of the paint, the preparation of the panel and the treatment of the drapery with works of known authorship and finds consistent habits. What kind of claim does that support?

options.text: A claim about the habits of a hand, which is real evidence but not proof, and can be overturned later
A proof of authorship, since consistent habits could never be produced by two different painters
options.misconception: believes stylistic consistency settles authorship by itself

options.text: A claim about the date of the work, since the same habits also establish when it was painted
options.misconception: takes evidence about a hand to be evidence about a year

options.text: A claim about the value of the work, since an accepted attribution raises the price by definition
options.misconception: assumes a scholarly conclusion has a fixed financial consequence by itself

questions.explanation: Attribution by connoisseurship works by accumulating consistent habits, and habits are evidence because painters repeat themselves. But the comparison is with an artist's output as we know it, which is itself partly an attribution, and the habits are imitable. New documents, new attributions of the comparisons, or technical results that redate the works being compared can all shift the balance, which is why attributions are stated with a degree of certainty rather than as verdicts. An acceptance is a scholarly agreement at a date, and it carries financial consequences, but the financial consequence is a consequence and not the argument.
questions.hint: Ask whether a pattern of habits is the same thing as a document, and what a later discovery could do to it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that resists its label
questions.learningObjective: handle a work that does not fit its category
questions.stem: A picture is routinely described as belonging to a named movement, yet it is symmetrically composed, carefully finished and free of the qualities normally used to define that movement. What should a description of that picture say?

options.text: That the label is convenient but the work does not exemplify it, and that both facts belong in the account
That the work is misattributed, since no painter of the movement worked in that manner at all
options.misconception: rules a work out of a movement on style alone and ignores the label's use

options.text: That the label is correct, since a movement is defined by who belongs to it rather than by how it looks
options.misconception: makes membership the test, which is what removes any chance of disagreement

options.text: That the work is an early piece by the founder, since founders always work against their own movement
options.misconception: turns a mismatch in style into a stage in a career, without evidence for it

questions.explanation: Labels are instruments, and like instruments they can be used well or badly. A movement name gathers works that share describable features, and it earns its keep by making those features askable. A work that does not exhibit them is a real problem, and the useful description is the one that keeps both facts on the page: the label tells a reader where to look, and the description of the work tells the reader what is actually there. Excluding the work on style alone loses it, accepting the label uncritically flattens the category, and turning the mismatch into a career stage is an invention.
questions.hint: Ask what a label is for, and what happens when the work does not fit the definition behind it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how style is used to date a work
questions.stem: A panel is unsigned and undated. A scholar collects the features that can be compared with documented works: the treatment of the eyes, the fall of the drapery, the ground beneath the paint, and the profile of the frame mouldings. What is that method doing?

options.text: Narrowing the date by matching a group of features against works whose dates are independently known
Fixing the date exactly, because a single drapery fold belongs to only one year
options.misconception: believes one feature is diagnostic of a year rather than of a range

options.text: Proving the attribution as well, since the same habits identify the painter and the year together
options.misconception: turns a dating argument into an authorship argument without separate evidence

options.text: Failing entirely, since stylistic features change too gradually to be compared with anything
options.misconception: assumes gradual change makes comparison impossible, which is the method itself

questions.explanation: Dating by style works like a bracket. Each feature is checked against works whose dates are established independently, by documents, and a feature that also appears in a securely dated work sets a limit of one kind while a feature that appears only after a certain date sets the other. The strength of the method comes from using several features together, since no single feature is diagnostic and fashions travel unevenly. Its weakness is the mirror image: a feature travels, so a single feature can mislead, and the frame is included in the survey because objects are dated as assemblages.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison needs on the other side of it, and how many features are being used at once.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what analysis of a wooden support can establish
questions.stem: A panel is reported to have a youngest preserved growth ring that falls in a range of years, and its timber has been identified as a type grown in a distant region. What do those two results actually establish?

options.text: That the panel cannot be earlier than that range, and that the timber had to be carried to the place of use
That the picture was painted in the year the tree was felled, since the panel was worked while fresh
options.misconception: turns a terminus into an exact date for the painting itself

options.text: That the painter worked in the region the timber came from, because the wood was always local
options.misconception: assumes a panel carries its tree to the studio of the painter who used it

options.text: That the picture must be a later copy, since an original panel is not made from measured timber
options.misconception: treats a scientific result as evidence of copying

questions.explanation: The ring measurement is made on the panel itself, so it belongs to the support, and the youngest surviving ring gives a latest possible date for the felling of the tree, allowing for the sapwood that is often lost. That makes it a terminus: the panel cannot be older than the wood allows, while the painting on it may be decades later. Wood identification is a separate and probabilistic result, used to argue about where the timber was cut and how far it travelled, and it is a strong clue about workshop and trade without proving where the picture was painted.
questions.hint: Ask whether the ring date is the date of the felling or the date of the painting, and what it is measured on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory report can date
questions.learningObjective: apply a material report to the date of a painting
questions.stem: A laboratory reports that a picture contains lead white, a copper green, and one synthetic organic colour that was not manufactured until after 1860. What follows from that report?

options.text: The picture was painted, or substantially repainted, after that date, quite possibly in more than one campaign
The picture must be earlier, because painters of earlier periods also used white and green pigments
options.misconception: lets two undated pigments outweigh one precisely dated pigment

options.text: The picture is a copy, since no original work contains a modern colour anywhere in its paint
options.misconception: jumps from a material date straight to a verdict of copying

options.text: Nothing follows at all, because a later campaign of overpaint leaves the date of the picture unchanged
options.misconception: ignores the possibility of repainting, which is the ordinary explanation

questions.explanation: Only the third of those results is a dating instrument, and it is a strong one: a pigment that did not exist cannot be in the original paint, so the layer containing it was made later. The most likely explanation is not a modern copy but a modern campaign, since repainting, retouching, varnishing and restoring have been normal events in the lives of pictures, and a laboratory samples layers rather than pictures. That is why the report is read together with a stratigraphic examination, and why a mixed result is reported as several events at several dates rather than as a single answer.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three reported pigments carries a date, and what else might have been done to an old picture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shared theme in two cultures
questions.learningObjective: state what a cross-cultural comparison on a shared theme reveals
questions.stem: Two works in different cultures both show a figure mourning over the dead, and the comparison finds the same subject treated as a public rite performed on behalf of a community in one and as a private act of devotion in the other. What has the comparison established?

options.text: That a shared subject is answered differently by each context, and that the differences are the informative part
That the work made in the richer culture is the more important version of the one idea
options.misconception: turns a comparison into a ranking of value between two traditions

options.text: That one of the two is a copy of the other, since the subject they share is identical
options.misconception: infers transmission from a shared theme, which travels independently of copying

options.text: That the theme is a borrowing, so the two traditions cannot be compared with each other at all
options.misconception: uses a shared subject as a reason to refuse comparison altogether

questions.explanation: A shared subject is a good place to begin, because it isolates the variable. If the theme is held roughly constant, then whatever differs in scale, medium, setting, audience and treatment of the body is doing work in its own context, and those differences are exactly what a comparison can reveal. That is the opposite of a claim that one version is the better one, since the two are answers to different problems, posed by different patrons, materials and rituals. The productive discipline is to ask what question each work was built to answer, and to let the difference stand as the result.
questions.hint: Ask what each work is doing for the people who commissioned and used it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why comparison is not a ranking
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a ranking claim made in a comparison
questions.stem: A study compares a large painted altarpiece made for a public church in one culture with a small carved figure made for private devotion in another, and concludes that the first is the more advanced work. What is the objection to that conclusion?

options.text: The two answer different problems set by different patrons and materials, so ranking them establishes nothing
The comparison is unfair because the works differ greatly in size, which is the only real objection
options.misconception: reduces the objection to a matter of dimensions rather than of purpose

options.text: The comparison is unfair because it used reproductions rather than the original objects throughout
options.misconception: makes the medium of examination the objection instead of the question asked

options.text: The comparison is unfair only if the two works hang in different museums rather than in one room
options.misconception: locates the problem in the display rather than in the claim being made

questions.explanation: A comparison answers a question, and the ranking in this study answers a different and much worse one, since the works were not competing for the same thing. An altarpiece for a public church is a large object, seen at a distance by a congregation, made in paint on a wall, and judged on what it does for a community over time. A small carved figure for private devotion is handled, carried, and met at close range by one person. Differences in scale, technique and finish follow from those uses, so a scale of advancement measures the uses and not the quality.
questions.hint: Ask what question each work was built to answer, and who asked it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what inventories and sale catalogues record
questions.stem: A court collection built over several generations is documented by inventories drawn up at the death of each ruler, and by sale catalogues published after the collection was dispersed. What do those two kinds of record tell us, and in what order?

options.text: What the family held and intended to keep, and then what the market made of it afterwards
Only what the family held, since a sale catalogue says nothing about who owned a picture
options.misconception: ignores the ownership information that a catalogue necessarily contains

options.text: Only what buyers paid, since an inventory records prices rather than the objects themselves
options.misconception: reduces an inventory to a price list and loses its main content

options.text: What the painters intended, since a collection is best read through the wishes of its artists
options.misconception: reads a record of ownership as a record of artistic intention

questions.explanation: The two records bracket the history of the collection. An inventory drawn at a ruler's death records what the family believed it held, and often what each object was for, which room it stood in, and how it was valued, so it is a statement of intention as well as of property. After a dispersal the sale catalogues record what reached the market, at what price, and described in terms aimed at buyers, which is a different kind of document with different interests. Read in sequence they give a collection a before and an after, and the gap between the two is usually where the interesting history lies.
questions.hint: Ask when each record was made, and what kind of event each one was recording.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the criteria that govern a restoration decision
questions.stem: A painting's surface is darkened by an old discoloured coating, and a conservator could remove that coating and make the colours strong and bright again. What actually governs whether it should be done?

options.text: Whether the removal can be limited, tested and reversed, and whether the state it conceals is itself of interest
Whether the colours will look stronger afterwards, since that is the only test worth applying
options.misconception: makes visual improvement the sole criterion, ignoring what the coating preserves

options.text: Whether the owner wants the picture bright, since the owner's wish settles the matter outright
options.misconception: hands a technical and ethical decision to preference alone

options.text: Whether the original painters cleaned their own pictures, since their habits should be the standard
options.misconception: seeks guidance in the practice of painters rather than in the needs of the object

questions.explanation: The decision is not about brightness but about the future. A removal that cannot be limited to a tested area, or that removes original material along with the discoloured layer, is not a treatment but a loss, and nothing in the future will bring back what has gone. That is why trial cleaning in an inconspicuous area, the smallest effective treatment, and a written record of what was done are the standing requirements. Alongside them sits a second question that the criteria above state: an old coating is part of the object's history, and a state that is legible as past may be worth more than a surface that looks as it did when it left the studio.
questions.hint: Ask what a later restorer would have to undo, and what evidence the coating itself carries.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a forgery has to match
questions.learningObjective: identify the hardest material evidence to imitate
questions.stem: A picture passes for an old master. It has convincing-looking cracks, an old frame, and a surface that has darkened convincingly over what appears to be centuries. Which of those three is the hardest kind of evidence for a copyist to produce, and why?

options.text: The material evidence, because a surface can be aged but the ground, pigments and support of a period cannot be
The cracks, because no one can produce a network of them without the original materials
options.misconception: believes crack patterns are impossible to imitate, when they are routinely induced

options.text: The frame, because a moulding of that period can no longer be bought or copied by anyone
options.misconception: assumes old mouldings are unobtainable, when they are made deliberately for the trade

options.text: The darkened surface, because dirt and varnish cannot be applied convincingly by hand at all
options.misconception: believes artificial ageing is not practised, when it is well documented

questions.explanation: Crack networks can be induced, darkening can be engineered with staining and varnishes, and mouldings are cut for the market in the styles that sell, so all three are available to a determined copyist. The ground, the pigments and the support are a different matter, because they are made at a particular time from particular materials with particular recipes, and analysis reads them directly rather than inferring them. That is the plainest reason physical analysis carries so much weight in authentication, and also why a forger works backwards from analysis, matching materials to a period and accepting the loss in the areas that cannot be examined.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three can be produced by a person working deliberately in a modern workshop.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The programme on a church portal
questions.learningObjective: read scale and placement as a programme
questions.stem: Above the doorway of a cathedral, a carved scene shows a central figure of judgement with the largest figure of the whole ensemble beside him, the saved and the condemned separated to either side, and, small at the base of each jamb, a kneeling donor holding a model of the church. What does that arrangement do for a person coming up to the door?

options.text: It states the order of the two worlds before the donor, and sets the donor at the threshold of both
It makes the figures larger in proportion to how far back into the carving they are placed
options.misconception: reads a ranking of importance as though it were a ranking of distance

options.text: It records the number of people who attended the consecration, since every figure is an attendee
options.misconception: treats the figures as a literal attendance list rather than as a scheme

options.text: It shows that the cathedral was built by a guild, since the donors hold models of the building
options.misconception: reads a votive object as a masonic signature

questions.explanation: The carving is a programme and the scale is its grammar. The largest figure is the most important presence in the scheme, and the two sides state the outcome of judgement, which is what a church door has to say to everyone arriving, whether or not they can read. The donors are small because they are not part of the judgement, and their models identify them with the building itself, so the gift and the giver are presented together. Reading the sizes as distances would require a picture with a consistent ground line and converging space, and this is a scheme of ranks rather than a view.
questions.hint: Ask what the difference in size asserts, and where the viewer is standing while reading it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A charter, a saint, and a gift
questions.learningObjective: infer the claim made by a ceremonial presentation
questions.stem: A painting shows a ruler handing a written charter to a kneeling abbot, while a figure in the heavens above places a hand on the ruler's shoulder. What does that arrangement assert?

options.text: That the gift is authorised from above and witnessed by a higher power, and is therefore meant to hold
That the church has absolved the ruler, so the charter is a private confession rather than a grant
options.misconception: reads a blessing from above as an absolution for wrongdoing

options.text: That the ruler's authority is the church's to give away, and the hand above claims ownership
options.misconception: turns a witness into an act of taking from the ruler

options.text: That the monastery is the donor, and the ruler is shown handing back something he once received
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the gift described in the scene

questions.explanation: The picture is a public record of an act with legal consequences, and its three figures divide the roles. The ruler gives, the abbot receives, and the figure above authorises, which is what makes the gift permanent in the language of the image rather than merely a transaction between two parties. Paintings of this kind were witnesses as well as decoration: a copy of a charter hangs with the document itself, and the image exists so that the terms are visible to anyone who comes. The hand from above is a warrant, not a claim on the property.
questions.hint: Ask who gives, who receives, and what the figure above the pair is doing there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A still life made to sell
questions.learningObjective: state what a market subject advertises
questions.stem: A still life shows a pocket watch, a heap of coins, a rare imported flower, a half-peeled lemon and a folded document, arranged on a table against a dark ground. Who was such a picture painted for, and what was it for?

options.text: The buyers in an open market, and it advertises the sitter's trade, credit and worldliness to them
A single merchant, as a record of exactly what stood on that shop's counter on one day
options.misconception: takes the picture to be a literal inventory of goods rather than a picture to sell

options.text: A botanist, as a record of a plant that could not be grown in the region where it was painted
options.misconception: reads an exotic subject as scientific documentation rather than as display

options.text: A guild, since only members of the traders' guild are shown with coins in these pictures
options.misconception: believes the subject functions as a qualification rather than as a claim

questions.explanation: The subject is chosen for what it tells the buyer about the person who owns it, and the objects are selected for what they carry: a watch and coins for the counting and credit of trade, a rare flower for the reach of the owner's suppliers, a document for a business in order, and a partly peeled lemon for a life of material comfort. That is a package aimed at purchasers, and such pictures were made in a market where the same subject appeared in many sizes and repeat versions, with the quality varying according to the time available. The picture is advertising, and it is also a claim about the world the buyer belongs to.
questions.hint: Ask who buys a picture like this, and what a buyer learns from the objects shown.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: interpret a catalogue provenance line
questions.stem: A museum catalogue entry reads: 'Provenance: 1790, in a named collection; from 1790 until 1912, private collection, location unknown; acquired by the museum in 1923.' What can a reader safely take from that line?

options.text: That the picture was recorded in 1790 and again at its acquisition, with an interval left untraced
That the ownership of the picture is documented without a gap for the whole period since 1790
options.misconception: reads an acknowledged gap as though the line had filled it

options.text: That the picture was made in 1790, since that is the earliest year named in the chain
options.misconception: mistakes the earliest documented owner for the date of the making

options.text: That the picture was sold in 1790, since a change of collection can only have happened by sale
options.misconception: assumes a single kind of transfer and ignores inheritance and gift

questions.explanation: A provenance line is a compressed record, and the useful habit is to read it as three separate claims. The first names a collection with a date, which is a document. The second covers a century and a month of ownership with no location given, which is a period of possession that nobody has traced, and it is a gap of a different kind from a break in the chain. The third is a transaction with a date. The line is honest about all of that, and a reader who wants to know more should ask for the inventory behind the 1790 entry and the sale catalogue behind the 1923 one.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the line name a documented event and which part is a holding of unknown detail.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a comparative wall text must do
questions.stem: A gallery hangs a carved figure of mourning from one culture beside a painted lament from another, and prints a text asking visitors to compare how each culture imagined grief. What has that label done, and what must it avoid doing?

options.text: It has proposed the comparison, and it must avoid turning it into a ranking of the two traditions
It has proposed the comparison, and it must avoid saying what the two works have in common
options.misconception: forbids a text from naming the shared theme it has just announced

options.text: It has settled the comparison, and it must avoid attaching a date or an owner to either object
options.misconception: claims the comparison is closed and so restricts the basic catalogue data

options.text: It has avoided the comparison, and it must avoid mentioning the material of either work at all
options.misconception: mistakes a request to compare for a refusal to compare

questions.explanation: A wall text that asks a question has proposed a comparison and left it open, which is the honest form for works from two traditions, since the visitor's own looking is part of the argument. What it must not do is convert that invitation into a verdict, because a verdict between two traditions turns a comparison into a ranking, and the two objects were built for different purposes by different people with different materials. Naming the shared theme, the dates and the materials is exactly what such a text should do; withholding them would be the opposite of caution.
questions.hint: Ask what the visitor has been invited to do, and what would spoil the invitation.

questions.topic: A painter's own account of himself
questions.learningObjective: distinguish self-presentation from later reputation
questions.stem: A painter's self-portrait shows him in his thirties, holding brushes, dressed plainly, with an inscription in his own hand describing his work. A portrait painted by another artist twenty years later shows the same man in rich dress with a knighthood displayed. What does that difference record?

options.text: Two different claims about the same man, of which the artist controlled only the first and made it himself
That the self-portrait is implausible, since a painter would not put his own tools on display
options.misconception: treats the presence of studio tools as a reason to doubt a self-portrait

options.text: That the second portrait is the earlier work, since a knighthood was an older kind of distinction
options.misconception: infers a date from the sitter's honours rather than from the painting

options.text: That the tools in the first portrait belonged to the master's workshop, not to the sitter at all
options.misconception: removes the props from the hands of the man who is painting

questions.explanation: The two portraits are two acts of self-definition with different authorship. In the first, the sitter is also the artist, so the props, the plain dress and the inscription are a statement he composed about his own practice, and they say that his work is what matters rather than his rank. In the second, the pose, the costume and the display of the honour are chosen by somebody else, and they say that the order he now holds is the thing to be seen. Read together they give the reception of a career in two takes, and the gap between them is the history of how a reputation was made.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the clothes, the props and the inscription in each of the two portraits.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: weigh surface appearance against material analysis
questions.stem: A painting offered as a fifteenth-century panel carries a fine network of cracks, a darkened surface and a frame of the right period. Analysis then finds the paint bound in a synthetic resin and containing a bright white that the laboratory dates to after 1920. What does the combination show?

options.text: The surface's convincing age is not evidence of age, since the analysed paint contains a material made later
That the picture is certainly genuine, since cracks, darkened surface and frame all agree with the period
options.misconception: lets appearance outweigh a precisely dated material result

options.text: That only the varnish was renewed in modern times, since varnish was the only thing ever replaced
options.misconception: assumes a modern material in the paint layer can only have come from a coating

options.text: That the picture is a modern copy, since a panel of that age could never have been repainted at all
options.misconception: turns a modern campaign of paint into a verdict that nothing original survives

questions.explanation: The two kinds of evidence work at different levels. Cracks, darkened surface and a period frame are appearances, and all three can be produced deliberately: crack networks can be induced, surfaces can be stained, and mouldings are cut for the market. A dated material is a measurement, and a pigment or binder that did not exist cannot be in a fifteenth-century layer. What the combination supports is narrower than either half alone, namely that the paint analysed is modern, which means the picture is not what it is claimed to be, while leaving open whether the whole object is new or an old one that has been reworked.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two kinds of evidence is inferential, and which of them is measured.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: interpret the wording of a museum attribution
questions.stem: A museum label reads 'School of Ferrara, fifteenth century', and the picture is shown in a case with works attributed to a named master from that city. What is that wording doing?

options.text: Assigning the picture to the group of followers of a master, and leaving the individual hand unidentified
Naming the workshop that produced the picture, and identifying the painter who ran the workshop
options.misconception: reads a school as a named shop with a known proprietor

options.text: Recording a former attribution to the master and confirming that the master painted the picture
options.misconception: believes a superseded attribution also confirms the hand

questions.explanation: A school attribution is a statement with three parts and one omission. It fixes a place and a period, both of which are claims that can be checked against evidence, and it places the work in the orbit of a named master, which is a claim about influence or training. What it omits is the individual hand, and the omission is deliberate, since to name a painter is a much stronger claim and one that can be withdrawn. Labels of this kind also record scholarly caution, and a picture moved out of a school into a named hand in a later catalogue has a documented history of argument.
questions.hint: Ask what the label says about the hand, and what it says about the place and the date.

questions.topic: A label that the handling contradicts
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a mismatch between label and handling
questions.stem: A survey places a picture among the painters of one named movement, on the strength of its subject and its palette. On inspection the paint is smoothly modelled in a finished academic manner with careful drawing, and none of the broken touch that the survey uses to define the group. What is the soundest conclusion?

options.text: The label and the handling disagree, and a description of the work should record both facts as they stand
The picture must be a later imitation, since no painter in the group could have worked so smoothly
options.misconception: concludes imitation from a finish the group has no monopoly on

options.text: The label must be right, and the survey's definition of the group is therefore wrong in every respect
options.misconception: lets a single disagreement discredit a whole definition at once

options.text: The picture must be a forgery, since its manner belongs to a period the group never practised
options.misconception: jumps from a stylistic mismatch straight to forgery

questions.explanation: A mismatch between a label and the object is a fact about the scholarship, and the useful description reports it rather than resolving it by force. Smooth, finished handling has been used to remove works from a group and to reclassify them, and it has also been used to argue for a later hand on a work everyone once accepted. Nothing in the mismatch by itself identifies the painter, dates the picture, or makes it a forgery, and a sound account will say which of the group-defining features are present, which are absent, and what follows from each. The record is the disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask what the mismatch establishes, and how many different explanations it leaves open.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a contract for a large work establishes
questions.stem: A document records a contract between a named master and a client for a large altarpiece. It names two assistants who will work on it, gives a total price and a subject, and sets a delivery date eighteen months later. What does such a document establish?

options.text: That the design, the price and the terms rested with the master, and that assistants contributed to the work
That the two assistants painted the whole altarpiece, since the document names them as its makers
options.misconception: reads a list of assistants as though it were a list of sole authors

options.text: That the master took no part in the painting, since the payment was made for other people's work
options.misconception: infers a total absence of the master's hand from a payment schedule

options.text: That the work was finished within a year, since a delivery date fixes the whole course of the work
options.misconception: reads a deadline as a record of the actual date of completion

questions.explanation: Contracts of this kind are unusually direct evidence for how a large work was made, and they support three conclusions. The price and the deadline fix the commercial terms, which tells a later reader what the work had to be worth and how long it had to take. The subject is recorded, which shows whether it was the client's requirement or the artist's proposal. And the naming of assistants confirms the division of labour directly, which is why such documents are the starting point for any argument about the hand. What the document cannot tell us is which passages the master executed.
questions.hint: Ask what the contract fixes and what it leaves open, and how a named assistant differs from a named master.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Testing a print against an inventory
questions.learningObjective: test whether a copy can be the work an inventory records
questions.stem: An inventory of 1651 records a canvas showing a lamentation, measuring 120 by 95 centimetres, with two angels in the upper corners. A print of 1790 shows a lamentation in the same proportions, but with a landscape behind the figures and no angels. What can a scholar conclude from the two records?

options.text: That the print is not a record of the 1651 canvas, since it lacks the two angels the inventory records
That the print is an exact record, so the two angels were removed before the print was made
options.misconception: assumes a copy is faithful to the work it claims to reproduce

options.text: That the inventory is mistaken about the canvas, since a print may not differ from its original
options.misconception: treats a disagreement between sources as proof against one of them

options.text: That the canvas was already lost in 1790, since a print cannot be made from a lost work
options.misconception: supposes a print requires the survival of the picture it reproduces

questions.explanation: Two independent records of the same kind of object can be compared feature by feature, and that is what an inventory is for. The inventory names the subject, the size, the medium and the subsidiary figures, and a print made two centuries later can be checked against all of it. Here the subject and the proportions match and the angels do not, which tells the scholar that the print is after a different composition, or after this one at an earlier state of it. Either way the print cannot be used as evidence of what the 1651 canvas looked like, and it may be evidence of a second work that the inventory does not mention.
questions.hint: Ask whether the print shows the features the inventory records for that canvas.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: interpret a price and volume series
questions.stem: A dealer's ledger records sales of one workshop's pictures over four years: nine pictures at four florins in the first year, fourteen at five in the second, twenty-two at seven in the third, and thirty-one at nine in the fourth. What does that sequence show about the shop?

options.text: That price and volume rose together, so the workshop had growing room and could work more slowly
That the shop was overproducing, since the last year's sales exceeded the first three together
options.misconception: treats rising volume as a symptom of overproduction rather than of demand

options.text: That price rose because the pictures grew smaller, since size alone sets a price in a market
options.misconception: invents a size trend that the ledger does not record at all

options.text: That the shop had no competition, since a rising price can only be the sign of a monopoly
options.misconception: reads a rising price as proof of exclusive control of the market

questions.explanation: Price and volume moving up together is the signature of a market with more demand than supply, not of a change in the size or the subject of what is sold, and a ledger is the plainest record of it. The consequence for the workshop is practical rather than abstract: with work selling steadily at a higher figure, the shop can afford to put more time into fewer pictures, and the quality of a later group may be visibly different from an earlier one. Ledgers are also the best evidence for dating a group of pictures, since an object can be placed against the years in which the shop was producing at that price and pace.
questions.hint: Ask what two things rising together tells you, and what a shop would do with that.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: weigh a partial provenance record
questions.stem: A provenance timeline reads: 1480 to 1520, a church in one city; 1520 to 1740, no record; 1740 to 1810, a merchant's house, listed in an inventory; 1810 to 1920, no record; 1920 onwards, a public collection. What is the effect of that record on an argument about where the picture was made?

options.text: Two intervals are simply untraced, so the argument rests on the documented periods and the rest is inference
The gaps prove the picture left the church and reached the merchant by an unlawful means
options.misconception: treats a gap in the record as proof of an illegal transfer

options.text: The gaps make the record worthless, so no claim about the picture can be supported on it at all
options.misconception: discards the two documented periods because two others are undocumented

options.text: The gaps prove the picture was stolen, since a lawful transfer would have left a record behind
options.misconception: assumes that a missing document can only mean a wrongful change of hands

questions.explanation: A gap is an absence of evidence, and it is not evidence of anything in particular. Nothing about the two untraced intervals indicates that the picture moved illegally, and plenty of lawful transfers leave no paper, since a gift, a bequest or a sale recorded nowhere leaves a trace in objects that is invisible to a search of documents. What a record of this kind does support is the argument that can be built from the two documented periods, the church and the merchant's inventory, with the rest stated as the unknown that it is. A provenance line written honestly is one that shows its gaps.
questions.hint: Ask what an absence of a record proves, and what the two documented periods still support.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify the intervention that fails a reversibility test
questions.stem: A treatment record lists four interventions: a surface cleaning done in a single campaign, tested in a corner and limited to the discoloured coating; the consolidation of one flake in the lower left with a synthetic resin; the retouching of nine small losses in matching pigment; and the removal of an old frame. Which of these is the one that a reversibility test would flag?

options.text: The consolidation, because a synthetic resin cannot readily be taken out later without the flake
The cleaning, because removing a coating can never be limited to the coating alone
options.misconception: believes no cleaning can be controlled, though the record states it was tested

options.text: The retouching, because paint used to fill a loss can never be identified again afterwards
options.misconception: assumes fills are undetectable, when modern pigments and raking light expose them

options.text: The removal of the frame, because a frame is part of the object and cannot be put back at all
options.misconception: counts a removable piece of furniture as irreversible damage to the picture

questions.explanation: Reversibility is the test of what a treatment leaves behind. A cleaning can be staged and limited, and the record says this one was tested in a corner and taken only as far as the discoloured layer, so it can be shown to have removed nothing original. A fill can be identified later, because modern pigments and raking light reveal it and because the record names the areas. A frame is furniture and its removal is recorded, so it can be reversed by re-hanging. A consolidant is the hard case, since a resin that has penetrated a flake cannot be taken out without the flake, and a future conservator is left with a choice between leaving it and losing the paint.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four acts adds a material that a later conservator would have to remove.
