questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: interpret a comparison table across two cultures
questions.stem: A study tabulates two works on a shared theme. Work A is a tempera altarpiece on panel, three metres high, made for a village church and used in a weekly liturgy, with the mourners drawn at the size of a person standing in front of it. Work B is a painted album leaf twenty centimetres high, made to be held in one hand, with a single figure shown at a distance. What does the tabulation show?

options.text: That the differences in scale, handling and audience follow from the two uses, and that both answer their purpose
That the larger work is the more serious of the two, since the scale of a picture measures its value
options.misconception: judges a subject by the size of the object carrying it

options.text: That the smaller work is a study for the larger, since the two works share a subject
options.misconception: infers workshop connection from a shared theme and nothing else

options.text: That both works came from one workshop, since a single hand is needed to treat a theme twice
options.misconception: believes a shared subject can only come from a single maker

questions.explanation: The fields of the table are the argument. Scale, medium and subject are not independent facts about these two objects; they are answers to the question each work was built to answer. An altarpiece in a church is seen from a distance by a congregation, week after week, and is therefore large, frontal and legible, and it is handled by clergy rather than owned by a viewer. An album leaf is held, turned, and read at arm's length by one person, so it can be intimate and can point the eye away into distance. Neither is a version of the other, and the table's value is that it makes that obvious.
questions.hint: Ask what each work was for, and what follows from the difference in the people who used it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A support and a pigment that disagree
questions.learningObjective: read a mixed laboratory report as a history of campaigns
questions.stem: A laboratory reports on a picture claimed to be of the 1480s: the support is a poplar panel whose youngest growth ring falls in 1501 or later; the ground is chalk and glue; the blue passages are bound in egg; and a bright white in the lower left is a titanium white, a material not manufactured before the 1920s. What follows?

options.text: The support and the binding suit the claim, while the white shows that one area was repainted later
Nothing follows at all, because a later campaign of paint leaves the date of the original unchanged
options.misconception: ignores that a modern material in the picture dates the layer it belongs to

options.text: The picture must be a modern copy, since no genuine panel can contain a modern white at all
options.misconception: turns a dated campaign of overpaint into a claim that nothing original survives

options.text: The picture must be an original of the claimed date, since a dated ring sequence settles the date exactly
options.misconception: treats a terminus post quem as though it were an exact date of painting

questions.explanation: The report has to be read result by result, and the results do not all point the same way. A panel and a chalk-and-glue ground are ordinary for the period claimed, and egg as a binder in blue passages is consistent with it; the growth ring sequence, read on the panel, sets a latest possible date for the wood without fixing a year for the paint. A pigment that did not exist cannot be in an original layer, so the white in the lower left belongs to a much later campaign of overpaint. The picture therefore has a history, and the correct statement is a history, not a verdict for or against the attribution.
questions.hint: Ask which results agree with the claim, which disagree, and what a modern white in one area means.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: From a stated purpose to a scale
questions.learningObjective: derive a format from the purpose of a commission
questions.stem: A contract says a picture will stand in a chapel, be seen by a congregation, and be lit by candles. First say what the stated purpose fixes, and then say what it implies about the size of the work.

options.text: It fixes the audience and the place of use, and those two together set the distance at which it must read
It fixes the price of the work, and the size is then left entirely to the painter's judgement
options.misconception: supplies a commercial term and ignores the conditions of seeing altogether

options.text: It fixes the subject alone, and the size follows from the subject with no reference to the place
options.misconception: makes the subject the only constraint and drops the conditions of viewing

options.text: It fixes nothing at all, since a commission is an agreement about money and about nothing else
options.misconception: denies that a contract states anything besides a sum to be paid

questions.explanation: A commission states the problem, and the problem is a viewing situation. A congregation in a chapel, lit by candles, sees a picture at a distance it is unlikely to measure, so the size, the contrast of the main figures and the clarity of the arrangement follow from that, not from any ideal of pictorial beauty. Contracts that survive often record the size as well, which is useful corroboration rather than a substitute for the argument. The painter is free inside those limits, and the negotiation about what to pay is conducted against them, which is why price and scale tend to travel together in the records.
questions.hint: Ask who will see the picture, from how far away, and under what light.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What raises and what lowers an attribution
questions.learningObjective: weigh evidence that raises and lowers an attribution
questions.stem: A work of uncertain authorship is being reconsidered. First say what kind of evidence would raise the attribution to a named painter, and then say what would lower it.

options.text: A document naming the work, or materials consistent with that master's practice, would raise it; a dated material his period excludes would lower it
A consistent style would raise it, and the same style in another work would lower it again
options.misconception: makes one kind of evidence act in opposite directions on the same question

options.text: A high price at auction would raise it, and a low price would lower it, since value follows attribution
options.misconception: derives an attribution from a market result, which usually depends on the attribution

options.text: A surface in good condition would raise it, and a damaged one would lower it, since condition shows a hand
options.misconception: believes the state of a surface identifies who painted it

questions.explanation: Evidence of the first kind is about the object and about its history: a dated document that names it, a record of its payment or its position in a collection, and analysis of its materials and support. A dated pigment or support that the proposed period excludes is the sharpest kind of counter-evidence, because it does not weigh style against style but puts the object outside the period in which the master worked. Evidence of the second kind, price, condition and auction result, is downstream of an attribution rather than a source of one, which is why a reattribution eventually moves the price rather than the other way round.
questions.hint: Ask which evidence concerns the object itself, and which merely reports an opinion about its value.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state a label's claim and read a work that resists it
questions.stem: A picture is described in a survey as belonging to a named movement, yet its handling and composition do not match the features the survey uses to define the group. First say what the label asserts, and then say what the mismatch shows.

options.text: It asserts a describable way of working, and the mismatch shows the label selects works rather than containing them
It asserts membership of a group, and the mismatch shows the group never had a style of its own
options.misconception: makes a disagreement about one work a claim that the whole group was style-free

options.text: It asserts a range of years, and the mismatch shows the range was fixed wrongly by the critics
options.misconception: reads a stylistic disagreement as a dating error in the survey

options.text: It asserts a set of subjects, and the mismatch shows the painter's range was unusually wide
options.misconception: turns a disagreement about handling into a claim about subject matter

questions.explanation: A movement name is a name for a describable way of working: a set of features in handling, composition, subject and function that a body of works shares. A label of that kind selects from a larger body of related work, which is exactly why a work can be related to the group and still not exemplify it. The useful description therefore holds two things at once, the name that tells a reader where to look and the handling that tells the reader what is there. Treating the mismatch as a verdict, in either direction, throws away the disagreement, which is usually the most informative part of the record.
questions.hint: Ask what a movement name is a name for, and what it is a name of.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the claim of a juxtaposition and the duty of a wall text
questions.stem: A curator places two works that have never been seen together and prints a wall text explaining the pair. First say what the juxtaposition asserts, and then say what an honest text has to do about that assertion.

options.text: It asserts a relationship the visitor would not have made, and the text must own the claim and name its limits
It asserts nothing at all, and the text must therefore supply the only interpretation available
options.misconception: denies that adjacency is an argument so the label must do all the work alone

options.text: It asserts a relationship, and the text must conceal that the choice was made by the museum
options.misconception: calls for the museum's own editorial decision to be hidden from the visitor

options.text: It asserts an ownership, and the text must record the price paid for each of the two works
options.misconception: mistakes a scholarly pairing for a statement about the two purchases

questions.explanation: Putting two objects together is an argument, because a visitor meets a sequence rather than a set and reads the adjacency as a claim about the relationship. The text exists to make that claim explicit, which means stating the grounds for it and stating where it is thin, and saying that the pairing is the museum's. What a text must not do is disguise the editorial decision, or present a curator's hypothesis in the voice of a settled fact, since the visitor cannot check it. The comparison is a reading offered for scrutiny, and the label is what makes it available for scrutiny.
questions.hint: Ask whether a visitor would have put these two works side by side without being told to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: sequence the work of establishing provenance
questions.stem: A picture has arrived at an auction with no history. Establishing where it has been is a sequence of steps, and each step depends on the one before. Put these five steps into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: The results are compared with published works, and an attribution and a date are proposed with their uncertainty stated
The object itself is examined, and its support, construction, frame, labels and condition are recorded
A chain of owners is drawn up from the documents found, with each link either cited or marked as a gap
The physical findings are tested against the documents, so that object and paper are checked against each other
Documents are searched for, among them inventories, sale catalogues, correspondence and customs papers

questions.explanation: The object comes first, because everything in the documents is a claim about an object, and a claim cannot be tested until the object has been examined and its labels, frame and construction recorded. The search of the archives comes next, and its result has to be set out as a chain in which each link is either supported by a citation or openly marked as a gap. The two bodies of evidence are then brought together, since a document is only as good as its agreement with the thing it describes. Attribution and date are the last step, and they have to arrive with their uncertainty attached, because a provenance is a finding, not a demonstration.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be known about the object before the paper can be made to agree with it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Establishing that a lost work existed
questions.learningObjective: sequence the investigation of a lost work
questions.stem: A painting is recorded in a seventeenth-century inventory, no longer survives, and a print made later is thought to be after it. Working out what can be said about it is a sequence of moves. Put these four moves into the order in which they have to be made.

options.text: Surviving copies, prints and photographs are compared with that description, noting every point of difference
A conclusion is drawn about what the evidence settles and about where it stops, in writing
The record is shown to be contemporary, so that the work's existence is fixed while it still existed
A chain of its owners is reconstructed from inventories and sale records, to show where it was and when

questions.explanation: The order protects the argument from resting on a document whose date is unknown. A record made while the work still existed is far stronger than a later mention, so that has to be established first, and it is what allows an owner or a location to be attached to a date. The chain of movements comes next, since it turns a mention into a history. Only then are the copies compared with the description, and the comparison is where surprises appear, since a print may be reversed, cropped, or show an earlier state. The written conclusion then states the boundary of what is known, which is the part a later reader needs most.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be established about the record itself before it can be used to date anything.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a conservation treatment
questions.stem: A painting needs treatment, and a responsible conservator works in a fixed order, because each stage limits what the next one can safely do. Put these five stages into that order.

options.text: The intervention is carried out in the smallest effective form, and the whole treatment is then documented
The condition is examined and photographed, and every area of loss, flaking and old repair is mapped
The proposed treatment is tested on an inconspicuous area, and the result is assessed closely
The damaged areas are consolidated, and each loss is judged on whether it should be filled at all
The materials are chosen for their reversibility, and what each one commits the object to is weighed

questions.explanation: Treatment begins by recording, because a map of the losses and the flaking is the only way to tell afterwards whether the object improved, and because handling decisions made before the condition is documented can destroy evidence. Materials come next, and reversibility is the criterion, since a consolidant that cannot be removed decides the question for every conservator who follows. The test in a concealed area then shows what the material actually does to this particular surface. Consolidation follows, and the losses are judged one by one rather than filled by default. Last comes the treatment itself, in the smallest effective form, and the written record.
questions.hint: Ask which stage has to come before any material is chosen, and which comes before the test.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a comparative study
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a cross-cultural comparison
questions.stem: Two works from different cultures treat a shared subject, and a study sets out to compare them without ranking either. That is a sequence of moves, and each one makes the next possible. Put these four moves into the order in which they belong.

The shared theme is defined precisely, so that what the two works have in common is not simply assumed
The comparison is published with its limits stated, and with no ranking of the two traditions
Each work is described in its own terms, with its patron, its audience, its material and its function

The differences can then be read as answers to different questions, which is the move that removes the ranking. Publication comes last, and carries the statement of what the comparison cannot settle.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a catalogue raisonné does to an attribution
questions.learningObjective: explain how a catalogue changes an attribution and its price
questions.stem: A catalogue raisonné of a single painter's work accepts some attributions and rejects others, and publishers say that doing so changes what the pictures are worth. Explain why a catalogue can move an attribution and a market value at the same time, and why neither move is final.

answer.exemplar: A catalogue raisonné is a scholarly attempt to establish the complete body of one artist's work, and it reaches that body by deciding case by case which pictures belong. Each entry carries the evidence for the decision, which is why the two outcomes move together: an inclusion is a claim that a particular object is by that master, and the claim is exactly what a buyer is paying for, so an accepted entry raises the standing of the object and a rejected one can remove the name from it. The value therefore does not rest on the paint, which is unchanged, but on the certainty with which the name can be attached to it, and markets follow that certainty closely and for a long time. Neither step is final, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of carelessness. The comparison works are themselves attributions, so the whole edifice rests on judgements that later evidence may unsettle; documents come to light, a red pigment turns out to have a manufacturing date, a panel proves older than the accepted career, or a new work turns up that shows a habit previously attributed to someone else. When that happens the catalogue is revised, sometimes drastically, and the prices follow again. The honest description of any attribution is therefore a claim held at a date, with its grounds stated, and the market value is a second-order fact resting on the first.

questions.explanation: A full answer has to make two links explicit, one from a catalogue entry to an attribution and one from an attribution to a price, and then say why each link is provisional. What earns credit is the recognition that the catalogue is the place where a body's works are argued over one at a time, that its inclusion and exclusion are judgements with reasons attached, and that the market prices the standing of an attribution rather than the picture directly. A weak response says only that catalogues are authoritative, or only that the market follows fashion, and never explains what the entry actually is.
questions.hint: Ask what the catalogue is a decision about, and what the price is a response to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain reversibility as the criterion of a treatment
questions.stem: A treatment can make a darkened painting look far better, and it can also be undone if it turns out to have been wrong. Explain why reversibility is treated as the governing criterion in deciding whether a treatment should be carried out.

answer.exemplar: Any treatment on an old object does one of two irreversible things. It removes something original, or it adds something new, and nothing added ages like the material around it: a resin that has penetrated a flake cannot be taken out again without taking the flake with it, and a fill stands in a loss for ever, visible under raking light to every conservator who follows. Those two facts make the future the deciding consideration. A conservator working now has an opinion about what a picture should look like, and that opinion will be revised, as treatments have been revised for two centuries; what cannot be revised is a decision to remove a layer that cannot be replaced. Reversibility is therefore the test of whether today's judgement stays today's judgement rather than becoming a permanent feature of the object. In practice the criterion produces a characteristic style of work. The condition is mapped before anything is touched, so that improvement can be measured against a record. The material is chosen because it can be identified later and, in the ideal case, taken out. Every material is tested in a concealed area first, and the result is assessed before the method is extended. Losses are judged one at a time and left open as often as they are filled, because an open loss is legible and a false fill is not. The treatment is kept to the smallest effective form, and the whole thing is written down, so that the next person knows exactly what was done and can undo it. None of that is timidity. It is the recognition that a treatment is an argument about the past, and that a later generation may well make a different argument with the same object in its hands.

questions.explanation: A full answer has to argue from the position of a future conservator, not from the appearance of the finished object, since the decision is made about an intervention whose consequences are unknown. What earns credit is the point that any treatment removes original material or adds material that will age differently from what surrounds it, that nothing now can guarantee how either will behave, and that an irreversible act forecloses the options of everyone after us. A weak response argues only from the improvement in appearance, or only from the risk of damage, and never reaches the argument about who decides for later generations.
questions.hint: Ask what a later conservator is left with, and what today's certainty is worth.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Naming a movement after the fact
questions.learningObjective: explain why movements are named retrospectively
questions.stem: Most named movements were given their names by critics or historians after the painters had stopped working together, and in several cases the first use of the word was hostile. Explain how that fact shapes the way the works of a movement should be read.

answer.exemplar: A movement name is nearly always a retrospective act, and understanding the act changes how the works are read. The painters involved did not sit down and agree on a programme; they exhibited together, argued with each other, and went on painting in different directions, and the group that later bears a single name was assembled afterwards by critics, dealers and historians who needed a way to talk about a shared origin. The word often entered as an insult, from a review mocking what was on show, and it became useful to the painters only once it had given them a position in the market and in the argument. A name of that kind is a description with a purpose, and it works by selection: it picks the features its author finds characteristic and leaves the rest out. That is not a reason to abandon the label, which remains the most efficient way of pointing a reader at a body of work, but it is a reason to ask what the label selects. A painter who shared an exhibition and a subject and nothing else may be inside the movement by date and outside it by practice, and a description that ignores that loses the most interesting thing about the work. The same applies to period names for earlier periods, and the effect on the paintings is the same in both cases. The name gives the works a company they did not choose, and the reader's task is to see both the shared features that justified the company and the differences the company suppresses.

questions.explanation: A full answer has to say who applied the name, when, and what that does to the reading of individual works. What earns credit is the point that a retrospective name is an argument about what a group has in common, made by people outside it and usually with a purpose, and that the name therefore selects certain features and leaves others out. A weak response says only that the name is inaccurate, or defends the label on the grounds that it is now conventional, and never asks what the naming did to the works it gathered.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the word, and what a name applied afterwards is selecting for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a comparison across cultures should not be a ranking
questions.stem: Two works in different cultures treat the same subject, and a study concludes that one of them is the more advanced. Explain why the comparison should be set up in a way that makes that conclusion impossible, and what such a comparison is then able to show instead.

answer.exemplar: The comparison has to begin from what each work is for, and that is what kills the ranking. An altarpiece in a church, a carved figure for private devotion, a painted album leaf to be held, and a relief cut into a city gate are answers to four different sets of conditions: a community assembled at a distance and at intervals, one person handling a small object, one person reading at arm's length, and passers-by moving past a public building. The patron, the material, the place, the scale and the audience are not decoration around the work; they are the reason the work has the form it has. Once that is granted, a single scale of advancement has nothing to measure, since a feature that answers one set of conditions perfectly may be irrelevant in another, and calling the difference a difference in quality simply relabels the difference in function as a difference in merit. The comparison is still worth doing, and it is worth more when set up this way. Hold the theme roughly constant, describe each work in its own terms, and then treat every difference as a finding rather than as a defect. What emerges is usually sharper than a verdict: how a community asks for permanence and how a private person asks for intimacy, how paint and stone and paper each answer a request, how a figure is made to be seen from below, from across a square, or from six inches away. A study built that way can tell a reader what each culture thought the subject was for, which is a larger result than a preference, and it leaves both objects more fully themselves than the ranking did.

questions.explanation: A full answer has to explain what the two works are each for, and then show that a single scale of merit cannot survive that explanation. What earns credit is the point that comparison becomes informative precisely when the variable, the subject, is held fixed and everything else, patron, audience, material, function, scale, is allowed to differ. A weak response says only that ranking is unkind, or only that every tradition has great works, and never supplies the alternative account of what the comparison can show.
questions.hint: Ask what each work was built to do, and who was going to see it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Height of a figure ranked above citizens
questions.learningObjective: compute a depicted height from a stated scale relationship
questions.stem: A relief cut for a civic hall shows a magistrate drawn at one and a half times the height of the citizens standing beside him, and the citizens are drawn at 1.6 metres. How many metres tall is the magistrate drawn in the relief?
questions.explanation: One and a half times 1.6 metres is 2.4 metres, so that is the height at which the magistrate is drawn. The arithmetic is easy and the interpretation is the point. The citizens are at the height of real people, which anchors the whole relief, and the magistrate stands fifty per cent taller, so the difference is a statement about rank rather than about the size of a real man. A picture that set out to be optically consistent would have made the magistrate no larger than a citizen standing in the same plane, and the two conventions are worth keeping apart. The scale is also part of the patron's message, since it asserts who outranks whom in a form that anyone passing the wall can read.
questions.hint: Ask what one and a half times 1.6 metres comes to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Attributions added between an inventory and a catalogue
questions.learningObjective: compute a change in the number of accepted attributions
questions.stem: An inventory drawn up in 1711 lists thirty-four sheets under one master's name. A catalogue raisonné published in 2020 lists ninety-six. How many sheets does the later catalogue add to the number the inventory recorded?
questions.explanation: Ninety-six less thirty-four is sixty-two, which is the number of sheets the later catalogue adds to the earlier count, and the difference is worth more attention than either figure. An inventory of that date recorded what the owner or collector believed he had, using a name attached by reputation rather than by examination, so the early figure is a statement of a kind of credit rather than a census. A catalogue raisonné re-examines every object and states the grounds for each decision, so a much larger total is a change in the standard of evidence as much as a change in what exists. The two counts also differ in kind, since drawings have been dispersed, rediscovered and reattributed, and a sheet newly traced to the workshop can be added without anything having been painted after the inventory.
questions.hint: Ask how many more sheets the new count has than the old one.
